gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's own MagGo 2 Pro FAQ rules out 25W on every Android phone (15W only, so a Pixel 10 Pro XL does not get 25W from the $109.99 pick), or that Apple caps the iPhone 16 and 16 Pro at 22.5W and the iPhone 17e at 15W.
standout_why: Compared against Macworld (cited), Anker's Qi2 25W blog (rank 1) and the TechRadar UGREEN review (cited; only its title loaded). Macworld already states that 25W needs an iPhone 16 or later on iOS 26, that older iPhones get 15W, that the iPhone Air tops out at 20W and that the 16e has no magnetic charging. In the part of Macworld I could read (first ~100k characters plus a keyword pass on the rest) there is nothing on Pixel or Android wattage, the iPhone 17e, or the 22.5W tier for iPhone 16/16 Pro. Anker's blog says only that older iPhones 'may charge at slightly lower speeds' and mentions Pixel 10 for a 15W model. The Verge (cited, titled 'for iPhone and Pixel') and pickedtech could not be opened, so The Verge may already cover the Pixel limit; that is why this is 2 and not 3.
decides: For iPhone 16 Plus, 16 Pro Max, 17, 17 Pro and 18 Pro owners the finding confirms ChatGPT's order: all four picks reach 25W, so the $55.99 Baseus AM52 stays the value pick. For Android owners it removes the Anker MagGo 2 Pro as the 'fastest sustained' pick: Anker says Android gets 15W, so the $109.99 fan-cooled model charges a Pixel 10 Pro XL no faster than a 15W Qi2 bank. For iPhone 15 and earlier, 17e (15W) and 16e (no magnets), no Qi2.2 bank charges faster than a cheaper 15W Qi2 one, e.g. INIU's own 15W SnapGo at $39.99. ChatGPT's closing line 'Older iPhones generally max out at 15W' misses the 17e, 16e, Air and 16/16 Pro tiers.

findings.label: Apple's peak wireless wattage by iPhone model
findings.value: 25W: iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, 17, 16 Plus, 16 Pro Max. 22.5W: iPhone 16 and 16 Pro. 20W: iPhone Air. 15W: iPhone 17e and iPhone 15 and earlier. 12W: iPhone 13 mini and 12 mini.

findings.note: Page dated September 18, 2026. It describes Apple's own 25W MagSafe Charger and does not mention third-party Qi2.2 chargers or an iOS version. The summary named only those seven models in the 25W tier; I did not see the full list, so other models (e.g. 17 Pro variants beyond these, base iPhone 18) may also be on it.

findings.label: Apple's limit while a wired accessory is plugged into the iPhone
findings.value: Wireless charging limited to 16W on iPhone 17 and iPhone Air, and 7.5W on iPhone 16 models
findings.source_title: How to use your MagSafe Charger with iPhone - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's wording: "limited to 16W for iPhone 17 and iPhone Air to comply with regulatory standards". Applies when a USB-C or Lightning accessory is connected to the phone during wireless charging.

findings.label: iPhone 16e and magnetic charging
findings.value: Apple lists the iPhone 16e as a non-MagSafe, Qi-compatible device
findings.source_title: How to use your MagSafe Charger with iPhone - Apple Support
findings.note: Consistent with Anker's '(Except iPhone 16e)' and INIU's exclusion. Macworld already states this.

findings.label: Pixel 10 wireless wattage by model
findings.value: Pixel 10 Pro XL: Qi2.2, 25W with a Qi2.2-certified charger and a 35W or higher adapter. Pixel 10, 10 Pro and 10 Pro Fold: 15W.
findings.source_title: The Pixel 10 phones go all-in on Qi2 with Pixelsnap, but one model's leading the pack (Matt Horne, Android Authority, 2025-08-20)
